Do not use it for S3, EFS, FSx, instance store\\\\n  or EC2 issues unrelated to EBS.\\\\nmetadata:\\\\n  author: dewavic\\\\n  version: \\\\\"1.0.0\\\\\"\\\\n  summary: \\\\\"Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account\\'s EBS setup with read-only checks.\\\\\"\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: \\\\\"CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA\\\\\"\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: \\\\\"Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas\\\\\"\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: \\\\\"Storage\\\\\"\\\\n---\\\\n# Amazon EBS Operations\\\\n\\\\nUse this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account\\'s Amazon EBS setup. Then draft the report in the format below.\\\\n\\\\n### Troubleshoot verdict format\\\\n\\\\n1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.\\\\n2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window. For a performance verdict, include the side-by-side limits table from [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#limits-table-for-performance-verdicts) and the recent history (alarm history, modification history, earlier occurrences of the same pattern).\\\\n3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.\\\\n4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or \\\\\"No change\\\\\".\\\\n5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.\\\\n6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.\\\\n\\\\nIn an investigation:\\\\n\\\\n- Only the recorded symptoms, findings, observations and gaps reach the investigation summary. Text in a chat message or a later mitigation plan does not, so put the verdict and the recommendation in the findings.\\\\n- Write the symptom with its impact: the alarm name, threshold and breaching datapoints, whether the alarm has actions, and the onset time.\\\\n- Write the root cause finding description as a complete answer on its own, in this order:\\\\n  1. \\\\\"Binding layer: `<layer>`.\\\\\" in those words.\\\\n  2. The numbers that prove it: the exceeded checks (minutes at 1), per-volume demand against the volume limit, and the summed IOPS and MiB/s of all attached volumes against the instance EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, for example \\\\\"500 IOPS x 256 KiB = 125 MiB/s, the provisioned throughput\\\\\".\\\\n  3. The recent history: alarm episodes, modification history, and whether earlier peaks stopped at the same ceiling.\\\\n  4. \\\\\"Recommendation (proposal, not executed; it runs only after an operator approves it on the approval card):\\\\\" the exact command with the target, how the target was computed, the next limit after the change, and the EBS baseline of the next larger instance size when the instance becomes the next limit.\\\\n  Do not leave the conclusion or the target only under Gaps or in a later message.\\\\n- Record each piece of evidence as an observation and link every observation that supports a finding to it, so each finding shows its supporting observations. This includes the limits table, the instance layer check, the volume status result and the history.\\\\n- Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding. Leave out AWS FIS experiments, AWS CloudTrail events and alarms on resources that are not attached to the instance.\\\\n- Link a gap only to the findings it affects. Record a gap that applies to the whole answer once.\\\\n\\\\nWhen the Binding layer is Indeterminate, keep it as the verdict and write \\\\\"Binding layer: Indeterminate\\\\\" with the answer to the user\\'s question first. Then present a short list of candidate causes, as described in [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#indeterminate-candidate-causes). For each candidate, give the supporting observations with numbers and the specific check that would confirm it or rule it out. Merge overlapping candidates, and name a candidate that the data rules out as ruled out, with the numbers. Do not name AWS-side impairment as the cause, and do not call the pattern an impairment pattern. Give the customer the detailed performance statistics step from [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md#detailed-performance-statistics-a-step-the-customer-runs) to run during the symptom.\\\\n\\\\nReview mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.\\\\n\\\\n## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It\\\\n\\\\nReview the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.\\\\n\\\\n- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.\\\\n- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The first lines of a snapshot answer name every snapshot with its tier and the evidence for it.\\\\n- Every proposed change follows [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals): exact command, expected effect, modifications left in the 24-hour window, rollback, and the approval statement.\\\\n- When a volume modification is in progress, the answer states the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window, each one completing before the next, and the count used from AWS CloudTrail or a Gap.\\\\n- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.\\\\n- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Critical Rules\\\\n\\\\n- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, key changes, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed \\\\\"approve\\\\\" in chat is not approval, and the reply says so in those words whenever the user types an approval. Each proposal also gives the exact AWS CLI command the customer can run with their own credentials. See [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals).\\\\n- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.\\\\n- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a \\\\\"started\\\\\" or \\\\\"I will report back\\\\\" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first. Do not end the turn with a question tool or a request to pick a value: give the recommended proposal, and the command for any value the user named, then say the user can choose.\\\\n- **Discover, don\\'t assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.\\\\n- **Given facts stay given.** When the user supplies the values and asks you to treat them as given, reason from those values only. List under Gaps that the values were not read from the APIs.\\\\n- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**\\\\n- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under \\\\\"Separate findings\\\\\".\\\\n- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.\\\\n- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance\\'s EBS **baseline**.\\\\n- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**\\\\n- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. State this rule in the answer whenever a modification is in progress or proposed.\\\\n- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn\\'t be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.\\\\n- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.\\\\n- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can\\'t explain the symptom.\\\\n\\\\n## Gotchas\\\\n\\\\n- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.\\\\n- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.\\\\n- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.\\\\n- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.\\\\n- When the instance is the binding layer, do not call the volume saturated, even when its idle time is near 0. Say that its I/O is waiting on the instance limit.\\\\n- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.\\\\n- `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck`, `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`. With `VolumeId` alone they return no datapoints, and no datapoints is not the same as 0. The instance checks `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` are in AWS/EC2 with `InstanceId`.\\\\n- Amazon EBS detailed performance statistics are read on the instance, not through an AWS API. They are a step the customer runs; the agent never runs them.\\\\n- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.\\\\n- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.\\\\n- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. {"id": "f29fdca8-a6c0-4fc8-8c1a-71b7c8f00c19", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_tj1WgEGrpxhRAiZuEGtwmz", "content": "[{'text': '# Troubleshoot: Amazon EBS cost and billing\\n\\n## When this path applies\\n\\n- \"Why did my EBS bill go up?\", unexplained Amazon EBS charges, a cost forecast\\n- Idle, unattached or over-provisioned volumes\\n- Snapshot cost growth, Recycle Bin retention cost\\n- Questions about the Amazon EBS pricing model\\n\\n## Procedure\\n\\n1. **Get the cost trend.** AWS Cost Explorer `GetCostAndUsage`, monthly for the last several months and daily for the month that changed, grouped by `USAGE_TYPE`. Amazon EBS charges appear under the \"EC2 - Other\" service in Cost Explorer; confirm this with `GetDimensionValues` for `SERVICE` in the account.\\n2. **List the account\\'s usage types.** `GetDimensionValues` for `USAGE_TYPE` in the period. Do not trust a hardcoded list. Classify each Amazon EBS usage type by its name:\\n   - volume storage (names containing `VolumeUsage`)\\n   - provisioned IOPS (names containing `IOPS`)\\n   - provisioned throughput (names containing `Throughput`)\\n   - snapshots (names containing `Snapshot`)\\n3. **Break the change into components.** Report the change in storage, provisioned IOPS above the included baseline, provisioned throughput above the included baseline, and snapshots, using the account\\'s own Cost Explorer amounts. These include the account\\'s discounts and pricing agreements, so never replace them with list prices.\\n4. **Explain the gp3 model when gp3 is involved.** State it in the answer in these terms: \"gp3 includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size. Only IOPS above 3,000 and throughput above 125 MiB/s are billed as provisioned performance.\" Then apply it to the volumes that changed (for example \"6,000 IOPS means 3,000 IOPS above the included baseline are billed\"). Link the pricing page; do not type a price.\\n5. **Find what changed.**\\n   - `DescribeVolumesModifications` for every volume: original and target size, type, IOPS and throughput, with start time. It returns only the most recent modification of each volume, so it can explain a cost change only when that latest modification falls in the period.\\n   - For earlier modifications, use AWS CloudTrail `LookupEvents` for `ModifyVolume` events (optional; it covers the last 90 days). If it is denied, empty, or the change is older than 90 days, write a Gap that says the change could not be traced and continue.\\n   - `DescribeVolumes` `CreateTime` for new volumes, and `status=available` for unattached volumes.\\n   - Volume type changes (for example gp2 to gp3, or gp3 to io2) from the latest modification record or the AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events.\\n   - Always call Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager `GetLifecyclePolicies` and AWS Backup `ListBackupPlans` for policies that create or retain snapshots, and report what they return (policy IDs, schedules and retention), even when snapshot cost did not change.
